> **Marcus** · cohort peer

My first instinct here was that `answer_correct` is just a bad metric. It is string matching — if the model says "March 2024" and the gold says "2024-03", the token overlap check fails and you score a zero on an answer that is correct.

Is this not simply a scoring artefact rather than a real failure?

replies.body:
> **Dana** · reviewer · owns the eval harness

Worth checking rather than assuming, because it is a real failure mode of that metric — just not this one. Here is how to rule it out in about a minute, which is the habit worth taking from this more than the answer.

```python
from nanorag.metrics import answer_correct

for r in rows:
    if r["question_type"] == "temporal" and r["answer_correct"] == 0.0:
        print(f"gold: {r['gold_answer']!r}")
        print(f"got : {r['answer'][:120]!r}")
        print(f"  exact-mode: {answer_correct(r['answer'], r['gold_answer'], mode='exact')}")
        print()
```

Read twenty of those. If the answers look right and only the formatting differs, you have found a scoring artefact and you should fix the metric.

**On this corpus they do not look right.** The answers are fluent, on-topic, drawn from the correct documents — and they do not contain the derived fact the question asks for. Scoring them by hand gives roughly the same number the metric does.

For completeness on the metric itself, since your objection is a good one and the answer is specific: `answer_correct(mode="contains")` normalises both strings, splits gold on non-alphanumerics, keeps tokens longer than two characters, takes the first six, and requires 60% of them to appear. For a gold answer of `"2024-03-15"` the surviving token is `["2024"]` — `"03"` and `"15"` are too short. So `"March 2024"` **does** score 1.0. The metric is more forgiving than you assumed. That is why it is not the explanation here.

> **Marcus** · cohort peer

Checked twenty by hand as suggested. Fourteen are fluent sentences about the right entities that never state a date relation at all. You are right, and my objection was the comfortable answer rather than the true one.

comments.body:
> **Rafael** · cohort peer · came from search infra

If retrieval is fine and the metric is fine, what is left is the generator — and I think the answer is that we are asking an extractive reader to do arithmetic.

`ExtractiveGenerator` is the default. It scores sentences in the packed context and returns the best one verbatim. A temporal question like *"which incident was resolved first"* has an answer that **appears in no single sentence** — it has to be derived by comparing two dates in two different chunks.

An extractive reader cannot produce a fact that is not literally present. So retrieval succeeds, packing succeeds, and generation cannot possibly succeed. Is that the whole story?

replies.body:
That is the whole story, and you have arrived at the most important distinction in the curriculum, so let me put a frame around it.

**The four verdicts.** "Retrieval problem or generation problem" is the two-bucket version people give in interviews. The useful version has four, because each has a different owner and a different fix:

| Verdict | Evidence in pool? | Survived packing? | Answer correct? | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Retrieval miss** | ✗ | — | ✗ | chunking, encoder, N, fusion |
| **Packing loss** | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ | `k`, reranker, packing constraints |
| **Generation failure** | ✓ | ✓ | ✗ | the generator, or the prompt |
| **Right by accident** | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ | **the scariest one** — model knew it without evidence |

Temporal questions on this corpus are squarely in row three. `evidence_recall 0.807` and `full_chain_recall` healthy say rows one and two are fine. `answer_correct 0.061` says row three.

**Why the repo ships this way rather than fixing it.** Swap in `AnthropicGenerator` or `BedrockGenerator` and temporal correctness jumps immediately — a real model does the comparison. That is a one-line change and it is documented in notebook 05.

It is not the default because **the default has to run with no API key**, and a curriculum whose first cell requires a credential is a curriculum most people never run. The cost of that choice is exactly the confusion in this thread: a metric that looks like a retrieval failure and is not.

**Which is the lesson, not the bug.** Row four is the reason to care. If you only measure `answer_correct`, an ungrounded model that happens to know the answer scores identically to a working RAG system. `UngroundedGenerator` exists in `generate.py` purely so you can measure that gap — run it and you will see a non-zero score with *no retrieval at all*. That number is your "right by accident" floor, and every `answer_correct` you report should be read against it.

> **Rafael** · cohort peer · came from search infra

The `UngroundedGenerator` baseline is the part I had not thought to run. Measuring what the model gets right with no context at all, and subtracting, is obviously the correct thing to do and I have never once done it.
